query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Utilizing a low‐temperature additive manufacturing route—specifically, 3D ink‐extrusion printing of AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock followed by controlled low‐temperature sintering—will markedly reduce residual thermal stresses and improve mechanical properties relative to conventional high‐thermal-load processes.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with a tailored particle size distribution and near‐optimal spherical morphology, as produced for conventional LPBF processes.
generation.intervention: Switch the manufacturing process from high-energy laser powder bed fusion to a room-temperature 3D ink‐extrusion printing method, followed by a controlled sintering step (e.g., below 800°C) in an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Miniature component geometries (1–10 mm) fabricated with layer thicknesses between 20 µm and 100 µm; printing performed near room temperature followed by sintering at temperatures <800°C under inert gas. Standard mechanical tests (tensile, compression, residual stress X‑ray diffraction) conducted at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The reduced thermal gradients during deposition minimize rapid solidification defects, resulting in a more homogeneous microstructure with fewer microcracks and residual stresses. Controlled sintering consolidates the build without reintroducing significant thermal load.
generation.mechanism: By avoiding the high-temperature, rapid melt–solidification inherent to LPBF, the process minimizes thermal shock and associated microstructural defects. The subsequent low-temperature sintering ensures consolidation while maintaining the refined microstructure, ultimately enhancing both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to components made under conventional high‐thermal-load regimes, the ink‐extruded and sintered parts will exhibit lower residual stress (as measured by X‐ray diffraction), fewer microstructural defects (observable by SEM/TEM), and a superior balance between strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Components manufactured by conventional laser powder bed fusion, which typically exhibit high residual thermal stresses, compromised mechanical properties, and complex processing requirements due to rapid melt dynamics.
generation.boundary: The benefits might be reduced if sintering conditions are not optimally controlled (i.e., if temperatures exceed ~800°C or if the ink formulation leads to incomplete consolidation) and may vary with the scale of the feature resolution in miniature components.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in residual stress reduction and mechanical performance is uncertain and depends on the details of the ink formulation, sintering kinetics, and environmental controls during processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components: one set using conventional LPBF and a second set using the proposed 3D ink‐extrusion printing followed by controlled sintering. Ensure identical geometries and comparable overall consolidation. Characterize the residual stresses, microstructure (via SEM/TEM), and mechanical properties (tensile/compressive tests) across both sets.
measurements: Residual stress measurements using X-ray diffraction
Microstructural analysis (grain size, defect density) via SEM/TEM
Mechanical property tests including tensile strength, ductility, and hardness
Porosity and consolidation assessment (e.g., via CT scanning)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ink‐extrusion printed and sintered samples do not show statistically significant reductions in residual thermal stresses and improvements in overall mechanical properties compared to the conventional LPBF samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

[ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications.
